title: The checker’s proof outside the machine
reason: This paragraph says the proof cannot be moved inside and invokes Gödel and Löb as the reason. Later the book explicitly says keeping it outside is a design choice and that these theorems do not forbid checking proofs about checkers. Bring the earlier passage into agreement with that narrower statement.

changes.before:
Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its trust rests
on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside the machine. I don't
think it can be moved inside, and Gödel's second theorem is my reason. The theorem says a
consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can't prove its own consistency, and a checker
vouching for itself would be doing something close to that. That last step is my reading. The
theorem itself stops at consistency. So I didn't get rid of the receipt
somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever reads the record. Try to move that proof inside the
system, so it can certify its own checker or a successor's, and you hit exactly the wall Eliezer
Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff named the Löbian obstacle in 2013, writing about agents that
want to trust their own rewrites. As I understand their draft report, they came at it from the
far side, an agent wanting to trust a successor's proofs the way it trusts its own. Same arrow,
pointed forward, same wall.
changes.after:
Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its trust rests
on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside the machine.
That's where I chose to stop this machine's chain of reasons. Gödel's second theorem does not
forbid a machine from checking a proof about a checker. It limits a sufficiently strong,
effectively axiomatized theory's ability to prove its own consistency, if the theory is
consistent. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff's 2013 draft on agents that trust their
own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can justify
trust in a successor's proofs. The relation is worth examining, but it does not prove that
my design is forced. So I didn't get rid of the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the
machine and handed it to whoever reads the record.

title: The name-and-renaming digression
reason: This is the longest passage whose subject is the tool’s identity. Recommend shortening it to the information readers need to identify the companion sources. It is an authored digression, so this cut is marked as a voice choice, not a factual correction.

changes.before:
The name is a joke three ways at once, and it's worth knowing before you say it out loud in
English. \emph{Coq} is French for rooster. It's also a nod to Thierry Coquand, a French computer scientist and mathematician, at the University of Gothenburg as of 2026, who worked out the
logic it started from with
Gérard Huet, a French computer scientist at INRIA, and to that logic's initials, CoC, for the Calculus of
Constructions; and there's a French habit of naming research tools after animals. The English
slang reading did what you'd guess. By the development team's own account, some people, women
students especially, ended up never learning the tool because of its name. So in March 2025 it
got a new one, the Rocq Prover, after Rocquencourt, the Inria site where it was first built,
and after the Roc, the giant bird of legend, so the bird stayed. Everything in this book was
checked with Coq 8.18, from before the rename, so that's the name I use. The rooster changes
nothing about what got checked.
changes.after:
The companion formalization uses Coq 8.18. The project was renamed the Rocq Prover in
March 2025; this book uses the older name to identify the version its sources were checked with.

title: What an accepted derivation establishes
reason: Compilation can succeed with an admitted statement, and a vacuous claim is not literally meaningless. Explain acceptance, assumptions and the translation problem accurately, without making either compilation or its rejection the definition of truth.

changes.before:
The compiler checks whether the types line up. If your proof has a hole, it rejects the proof, unless you write ``trust
me'' (the keyword is Admitted), and then it marks the theorem as unproved. But here's the part that matters: the
compiler checks that the proof matches the \emph{statement}. It does not check that the statement
says what you \emph{meant}. Hand it a statement that means nothing and it'll prove it for you,
three characters, no complaint. So a proof being accepted is not the same as the thing being
true. It means this proof matches this statement, and whether that's the right statement is
on me. The machine can't tell. \hyperref[sec:point]{The point} said a short version of this and I'm saying it again because every section
since has leaned on it: the checked names in this book are a promise that the \emph{proof} is
there, and the sentences around them are my claim about what the statement \emph{says}, and the
second can be wrong while the first is fine, which is why so many sections of this book
stop to say exactly what a statement's hypotheses are.
changes.after:
The checker tests a proposed derivation against its statement, under the definitions and
assumptions it uses. Admitted skips the derivation and turns the statement into an assumption;
the file can still compile. That is why a successful build alone does not show that every
claimed result has been proved. Even a complete derivation can settle the wrong question.
A statement can be true for an empty reason, such as a condition nothing satisfies.
Whether it expresses what I meant remains my responsibility.
\hyperref[sec:point]{The point} said a short version of this: the source names identify
formal statements and their derivations, and the sentences around them are my account of
what those statements establish. Comparing the two means reading the definitions, the
premises and the conclusion. The checker does not do that reading for us.
